clinicalPearls: A late-onset, autosomal dominant distal myopathy caused by variants in the ZASP gene (LDB3), now regarded as part of the myofibrillar myopathy spectrum (a ZASPopathy).
Onset is typically in mid-to-late adulthood with distal lower-limb weakness, characteristically the anterior tibial compartment (foot drop), before spreading to hands and proximal muscles.
ZASP is a Z-disc protein that binds alpha-actinin and stabilises the sarcomeric Z-line, and its dysfunction drives progressive myofibrillar disintegration.
Cardiac involvement (cardiomyopathy and conduction disease) and a mild peripheral neuropathy may accompany the myopathy, as with other myofibrillar myopathies.
Muscle biopsy shows myofibrillar pathology with Z-disc streaming, focal myofibrillar dissolution, cytoplasmic and spheroid bodies, rimmed vacuoles and ectopic desmin, myotilin and alpha-B-crystallin.
Electromyography reveals myopathic units frequently intermixed with abnormal spontaneous activity, and in some cases myotonic or pseudomyotonic discharges.
Skeletal muscle MRI shows a selective, often asymmetrical pattern of fatty replacement that helps distinguish it from other distal myopathies.
Diagnosis is confirmed by an LDB3/ZASP pathogenic variant, with cardiac and respiratory surveillance forming part of ongoing care.
reference.pathophysiology: ZASP (Z-band alternatively spliced PDZ-motif protein), encoded by LDB3, is a cytoskeletal protein of the striated-muscle Z-disc that, through its PDZ and LIM domains, binds alpha-actinin and other Z-line components to anchor the actin thin filaments and maintain sarcomeric integrity during contraction. Pathogenic variants, which tend to cluster in particular exons, are thought to act through a dominant mechanism that destabilises the Z-disc and promotes aggregation of Z-disc and intermediate-filament proteins. The consequence is a myofibrillar myopathy: focal dissolution of myofibrils beginning at the Z-disc, disorganisation of the sarcomeric lattice, and accumulation of degradation products and ectopic proteins such as desmin, myotilin, filamin C and alpha-B-crystallin, together with autophagic rimmed vacuoles. Because the same Z-disc machinery operates in cardiac muscle, some patients develop cardiomyopathy and conduction abnormalities, while involvement of the peripheral nerve axon or its terminal may underlie the neuropathic features seen in a subset. Progressive loss of functioning contractile units produces the slowly advancing distal-onset weakness that characterises the Markesbery-Griggs phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Other myofibrillar myopathies (desminopathy, myotilinopathy, filaminopathy, alpha-B-crystallinopathy, BAG3-related)
Miyoshi and other dysferlin-related distal myopathy
Udd distal myopathy (tibial muscular dystrophy, titin-related)
Sporadic inclusion body myositis in older adults with distal and quadriceps involvement
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase, usually mildly to moderately raised
Muscle biopsy with myofibrillar histology and immunohistochemical protein-aggregate staining
Whole-body or targeted skeletal muscle MRI
Molecular genetic testing of LDB3/ZASP and a myofibrillar myopathy gene panel
Cardiac assessment with electrocardiography, ambulatory monitoring and echocardiography, with cardiac MRI where indicated
Respiratory function testing including erect and supine spirometry
redFlags: Syncope, presyncope or palpitations suggesting cardiac conduction disease
New or progressive breathlessness, orthopnoea or morning headache indicating respiratory muscle weakness
Rapidly progressive weakness or new dysphagia
Family history of sudden cardiac death
reference.prognosis: Markesbery-Griggs distal myopathy is slowly progressive, causing accumulating distal and later more generalised weakness over years to decades, while life expectancy is often preserved. Prognosis is influenced chiefly by cardiac conduction disease and cardiomyopathy, and by respiratory muscle involvement, which warrant regular surveillance.
pitfalls: Mislabelling as another distal myopathy or as inclusion body myositis without genetic confirmation
Overlooking potentially life-threatening cardiac conduction disease and cardiomyopathy
Missing respiratory muscle weakness, which can develop before it becomes symptomatic
Attributing abnormal spontaneous electromyographic activity to a primary neurogenic disorder
Assuming a negative family history excludes a dominant condition, given variable expressivity and de novo variants
management: No disease-modifying pharmacotherapy; management is supportive with physiotherapy and occupational therapy to preserve mobility and manage progressive distal weakness
Ankle-foot orthoses and mobility aids for the anterior tibial weakness and foot drop

Regular cardiac surveillance with electrocardiography, ambulatory monitoring and echocardiography for cardiomyopathy and conduction disease, with pacemaker or defibrillator implantation when conduction block or arrhythmia develops
Respiratory monitoring with serial spirometry including supine measurements, introducing non-invasive ventilation when respiratory muscle weakness causes hypoventilation
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular follow-up coordinating neurology, cardiology and respiratory care
Genetic counselling and cascade screening of relatives given autosomal dominant LDB3/ZASP inheritance
Escalate urgently for cardiac assessment if syncope, palpitations or symptoms of heart failure arise
